extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, early-career faculty, grant writers and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points about how the NIH 'Innovation' review criterion is understood and used by reviewers, and practical advice for applicants on how to present innovation in an NIH grant application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (criterion meaning and weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is a distinct review criterion that NIH leadership emphasizes, but reviewers may resist privileging it over Approach and Significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues reviewers are not confused about what innovation means but may resist the notion that Innovation should be more important than Approach and Significance. Applicants should treat Innovation as a separate feature of the application to be explicitly addressed in the innovation section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers may downplay Innovation when they like Approach/Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: When you see some gibberish in the Innovation section of the critique written by your fellow reviewers you do not conclude they are fools. You conclude, quite rightly, that the reviewer liked an application that lacks any sign of innovation for other reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that reviewers who favor a project's approach or significance might give a weak Innovation write-up rather than downgrade the overall impact; this explains weak correlation between Innovation scores and Overall Impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-innovation work is valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that NIH funded science should be all Innovation, all the time is idiocy. We’d never get anywhere without people doing the unglamorous work to follow up, verify, utilize, translate, generalize, extend and connect with the most innovative science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only highly novel work is fundable; studies that follow-up, validate, translate, or extend important findings are legitimate and important even if not 'innovative' in the flashy sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant responsibility: explicitly argue why the project is innovative
rubrics_metrics.description: Your job as a grant writer is to offer up your best analysis of why your project innovates - in the new format you have an entire section to talk about your innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dedicated Innovation section to state clearly how your project is innovative. Present the strongest, concise argument you can; reviewers may or may not accept it, but you must make the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, declarative innovation statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications that do best on innovation only have one or, at most, two paragraphs in the innovation section. And these paragraphs comprise simple declarative sentences that recite the features of the proposed studies that are innovative and what makes them innovative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer short, simple declarative sentences (one–two paragraphs). A long-winded complex argument to make the case for innovation is an anti-pattern and may signal either lack of innovation or poor ability to make the case effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable forms of innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is variation in what reviewers consider innovation (e.g., 'a new paradigm in a field, tested with established techniques, is still innovative').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different reviewers/study sections may accept different types of novelty — conceptual (new paradigm), methodological (new method), or application/translation of existing methods to new problems. Explicitly state which type you claim and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reviewer and study-section variability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no instruction in how to write a grant application that will absolutely guarantee funding. It is a feature, not a bug, in the system that peer reviewers are variable, real world judges and not computer programs with a single set of well defined criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize variability across reviewers and study sections: some sections revere innovation, others ignore it. Don't expect uniform interpretation; tailor arguments and submission targets accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match submission to study-section culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep sending proposals to the most relevant study section (or three) so as to learn about the expectations of that study section when it comes to a proposal. Talk to colleagues that have also sent proposals reviewed in that section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the cultural tendencies of standing study sections (their biases about innovation vs. approach/significance) and adapt applications to nudge odds in your favor—choose sections, frame innovation, and revise based on feedback from peers familiar with that section.
